reading.title: Chapter overview
paragraphs: HarborInventory turns the previous lessons into a small, usable command-line program. It accepts equipment records, rejects duplicate identifiers and invalid quantities, lists the accepted inventory, and reports the total quantity. The goal is a complete, bounded application whose behavior can be explained and tested—not a collection of disconnected syntax demonstrations.

The source is divided into a domain library and an interface. The library does not read the terminal or print diagnostics. The interface translates text commands into library operations and reports results. That division lets tests exercise the rules independently of interactive input.

The capstone is where isolated language features become a design that another person can inspect. HarborInventory has a small command vocabulary, one clear owner of its records, and measurable acceptance conditions. The application does not need inheritance, templates, threads, or a graphical interface to demonstrate sound C++ foundations. It needs the simpler features to cooperate without hidden assumptions.

Treat the application as a chain of boundaries: input bytes become parsed candidates; candidates are checked against domain rules; approved operations change owned state; observers produce results; and tests establish whether the entire chain behaved as specified. A defect at one boundary should not require guessing about every other boundary.

Learning outcome. Build and explain a complete multi-file program, translate requirements into tests, distinguish parsing from domain validation, preserve state after rejection, and present evidence of what the finished application actually does. The final acceptance report should be candid about excluded features rather than describing future aspirations as implemented capabilities.

reading.title: 20.2.1 Dividing Responsibilities Across Classes and Functions
paragraphs: The inventory library validates records and owns accepted state. The command loop parses one line at a time, ensuring that a failed command does not leave a stream in a confusing partially consumed state for the next command. Reporting is a separate function that formats existing records without changing them.

Parsing produces a local candidate record. Only a fully parsed command is passed to the inventory. The library then validates domain rules before committing the insertion. This creates two boundaries: text syntax and domain validity. A command can be syntactically valid while still attempting a duplicate identifier, and those cases should remain distinguishable in tests.

The program separates the domain library from the command-line adapter. Inventory::add decides whether a candidate record may enter the collection. It does not ask the user for a replacement value or print a message. The adapter parses a line, calls the library, and chooses the diagnostic text. This separation keeps domain behavior testable without a terminal session.

Validation should occur before mutation. The library checks the candidate’s identifier, name, quantity, collection capacity, and duplicate status before calling push_back. Rejected candidates therefore do not change the accepted-record count or total. Tests must inspect state after rejection, because a false return value alone would not expose an implementation that modified the vector first.

The add parameter is passed by value. It represents a local candidate the function may transfer into storage on success. The implementation uses std::move at the insertion point, allowing suitable members to transfer their resources. This is a preview of Book II’s move semantics, not a statement that the word move physically relocates arbitrary objects or guarantees zero work.

When a caller supplies an lvalue record to a by-value parameter, the local candidate is ordinarily a copy of that caller-owned value. Moving from the candidate does not mean the caller’s original object was moved from. At other call sites, a temporary candidate may avoid that initial copy. Ownership decisions should follow the actual parameter boundary rather than the presence of a familiar utility name.

The input adapter uses a fresh std::istringstream for each line. Parsing failure on one command therefore does not leave the next line’s parser in the failed state. This is a practical reason to isolate line parsing instead of attempting to repair a single long-lived parser after every malformed token.

std::quoted allows a name containing spaces to occupy one logical field. It also accepts an unquoted token according to its extraction behavior. The protocol is not a complete CSV format and should not be described as one. Escaping and quoting behavior belongs to the chosen stream operation; arbitrary commas do not create fields automatically.

The comparison between chapters shows how a stronger grammar requires an explicit stronger validation step.

A const reference at the library boundary helps the compiler enforce that intent. A useful extension is a lookup operation. Returning a record copy gives the caller independent data but incurs copying. Returning a const pointer avoids that copy but creates a borrow whose validity depends on the inventory and its modifications. Either can be justified if the contract is explicit. Do not return a mutable reference that allows callers to rewrite an identifier and bypass uniqueness checks.

A quantity-update operation should locate the target, validate the new value, and assign only after validation succeeds. Rejected updates must preserve the old quantity and total. This is the same validation-before-commit pattern used for insertion, now applied to an existing record. The operation should not remove the record and attempt to reinsert it unless that more complex transaction is actually necessary.

Persistence would introduce a different class of requirement: file format, versioning, partial-write handling, replacement strategy, and recovery after interruption. Do not add a casual destructor write and declare the application durable. The final exercise asks you to design the boundary before implementing a storage feature that would need substantially more testing.

The capstone ends when the current contract is clear, implemented, and reproducible. It does not need every feature in the six-volume curriculum. A deliberately bounded application is a better foundation for later modern C++, algorithms, and systems engineering than an unfinished framework that nobody can fully explain.

cards.question: Does a const vector reference make retained element references permanent?
cards.answer: No. It restricts ordinary mutation through that reference, but element lifetime and invalidation still depend on the owning vector’s operations and destruction.

cards.question: Does a successful session exit mean every add succeeded?
cards.answer: No. Interactive command rejection is reported within the session while the program continues. Check the appropriate output as well as the process status.

cards.question: What is the final engineering outcome?
